title: Several papers in this collection combine photoredox catalys

messages.content: Several papers in this collection combine photoredox catalysis with a transition metal co-catalyst such as nickel, copper, or palladium. In these dual catalytic systems, what is the proposed mechanistic role of the metal cycle, and how does it interact with the photocatalytic cycle to enable bond formations that neither catalyst achieves alone? Are there recurring mechanistic motifs such as oxidative addition or reductive elimination gated by radical intermediates that appear in multiple papers?

**Background**

Dual catalysis refers to the strategic integration of two independent reaction cycles—typically visible-light photoredox catalysis and conventional transition-metal catalysis—to enable chemical transformations that neither pathway can achieve on its own. While photoredox systems use photon absorption to drive single-electron transfers and generate reactive radical intermediates, traditional transition-metal cycles rely on stepwise two-electron redox processes such as oxidative addition and reductive elimination. Synchronizing these fundamentally different mechanistic pathways allows chemists to construct complex molecular architectures under exceptionally mild conditions, establishing combined photocatalytic and organometallic strategies as a central pillar of contemporary synthetic methodology.

---

Based on the provided summaries, the transition metal cycle (predominantly nickel in the cited studies) functions as a radical-interception manifold that mediates formal two-electron bond-forming events while cycling through well-defined oxidation states (Ni⁰, Niᴵ, Niᴵᴵ, Niᴵᴵᴵ). It interacts with the photocatalytic cycle through light-induced single-electron transfer (SET) processes that accomplish two simultaneous objectives: generating discrete radical species from stable precursors (e.g., carboxylic acids, dihydropyridines, or silanes) and shuttling electrons to reduce higher-valent metal intermediates back to their catalytically active low-valent states. This tight electronic integration eliminates the need for stoichiometric metallic reductants (such as Zn or Mn powders traditionally required for cross-electrophile couplings) and enables otherwise inaccessible bond constructions (e.g., C(sp³)–C(sp²), C–N, and amide linkages) under mild, redox-neutral conditions.

Several recurring mechanistic motifs tied to radical-gated metal cycles appear consistently across the literature:
• **Radical-Gated Initiation Converging on High-Valent Intermediates:** As detailed by Kammer et al. (2021), photogenerated alkyl radicals engage the nickel cycle via two competing initiation pathways: direct combination with Ni⁰ to form Niᴵ prior to oxidative addition (OA) with aryl halides, or addition to pre-formed aryl-Niᴵᴵ species. Both routes funnel into a high-valent Niᴵᴵᴵ intermediate. Doyle corroborates this motif by demonstrating that Ni(I) complexes undergo oxidative addition to electrophilic substrates like aziridines, with stereochemical erosion supporting either an irreversible, stereoablative OA proceeding via SET or a stereospecific OA followed by rapid racemization at the Ni(III) stage.
• **Reductive Elimination as the Bond-Forging Step:** Following radical capture and oxidative addition, the coupled manifold relies on reductive elimination (RE) from the high-valent metal center to deliver the cross-coupled product and release a lower-valent metal species (Niᴵ). This step is structurally gated by the presence of the newly installed radical-derived ligand alongside the original electrophilic partner.
• **Photocatalytic Metal Regeneration via SET:** The active metal state is exclusively restored through photoinduced electron transfer rather than chemical reductants. Kwak et al. (2022) show that supported Ni single atoms dynamically shift oxidation states to interconnect with photogenerated electrons and holes on a carbon nitride semiconductor, establishing a continuous heterogeneous photoredox cycle. Similarly, Kammer et al. (2021) utilize an organic photoredox donor (photoexcited Hantzsch ester within an EDA complex) to reduce Niᴵ back to Ni⁰, with measured redox potentials (−1.17 V for the Niᴵ/Ni⁰ couple) confirming thermodynamically favorable electron shuttling.
• **Kinetic Competition Against Side Reactions:** Successful coupling requires that radical interception at the metal center kinetically outruns parasitic pathways. Stoichiometric investigations reveal that radical addition to aryl-Ni(II) intermediates must outcompete hydrogen atom abstraction from the photoactive hydride donor, dictating catalyst choice and reaction concentration profiles (Kammer et al., 2021). Additionally, some dual systems circumvent net oxidative/reductive requirements entirely by operating through redox-neutral cascades driven by in situ ring-opening transformations (Baussière et al., 2023).

While the provided summaries comprehensively delineate nickel-centered dual catalytic cycles featuring photoredox electron shuttling, radical-gated oxidative addition, and reductive elimination, they do not offer mechanistic insights for the referenced copper or palladium systems, nor do they present time-resolved spectroscopic or computational data characterizing the transient organometallic intermediates.
